title: Russell reacts after losing out to Antonelli in Italian GP
excerpt:
George Russell has given his take on an eventful Italian Grand Prix in which he lost out on victory in the latter stages to team mate Kimi Antonelli, with the Briton admitting that his team mate’s pit stop during the Virtual Safety Car phase “surprised” him.

Russell had looked in strong form throughout much of the race, having taken the lead early on from polesitter Pierre Gasly while Antonelli faced the challenge of working his way forwards from his P19 grid slot.

However, having rapidly making gains, the Italian was soon in the thick of the action at the front and engaged in a close battle with Russell for the lead.

When a Virtual Safety Car was called after Lance Stroll’s Aston Martin came to a halt, Mercedes pitted Antonelli for fresh tyres while Russell remained out on track. This initially dropped the championship leader backwards, but he again climbed up the order again and returned to second place.

Just a few laps from the end of the race, Antonelli finally found a way past Russell and held on to seal victory, with Russell having to settle for P2.

Despite his disappointment at missing out on the win, the British driver praised his team mate’s performance and admitted that it was a relief to claim a solid result after some ups and downs towards the end of the first half of the season.

“Huge congratulations to Kimi of course – an incredible result from him,” said Russell. “When I looked on the leaderboard at the beginning and I saw he was already in P5, P4, I knew straight away he was going to be in the mix. Huge congrats to him.

“It was looking like a pretty strong race from us and then I was just struggling with the tyres towards the end – obviously we did the whole race on that one hard tyre.

“I'll take it, it's been more positive than it was pre-summer break and that's what I needed to try and achieve. Of course I would have loved to be P1 today.”

Pushed on whether there had been any discussion about whether he would pit under the VSC, Russell responded: “To be honest I thought we were both going to stay out. I was surprised to see him pit.

“I think at the end it was a roll of the dice both ways. In the moment, the team wouldn't have known which strategy was better. It made sense to split the cars but, in the end, Kimi had great pace, and there we are.”

While the result means that Antonelli has extended his lead in the Drivers' Championship to 66 points, Russell has strengthened his hold on second place over Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton.

title: Antonelli's Italian GP victory a 'dream coming true'
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli admits his sensational victory in the Italian Grand Prix from P19 on the grid was like a "dream coming true".

Antonelli's prospects of a first victory on home soil at Monza seemed unlikely ahead of Sunday's 53-lap race, with the Italian starting towards the back of the grid after taking new power unit components.

But after the race was red flagged early after Charles Leclerc's dramatic crash at the final corner, Antonelli had already reached P12 and quickly scythed through the order at the restart.

Battling Merecedes team mate George Russell for the lead, Antonelli was brought into the pits under a mid-race Virtual Safety Car, before using fresher tyres to catch and pass the Briton with four laps remaining.

"Unbelievable, I'm so happy and I could never have imagined to be here today but we managed to pull it off and I'm really happy," said Antonelli immediately after the race, who added "it's a dream coming true".

"After the second restart I was up there and I knew I could have a shot for the win. Definitely I believed in it, especially when I was behind George but it was really difficult because it was really difficult to break away with the tow being so strong.

"At the end, we pitted and he [Russell] stayed out and he struggled a bit with his tyres at the end. With fresher tyres I was able to increase the pace and managed to win it."

The victory at Monza is the first for an Italian driver since Ludovico Scarfiotti in 1966, with P19 the second-ever lowest starting position a Grand Prix has been won from in Formula 1 history.

Antonelli's seventh win of the season moves him 66 points clear of Russell in the drivers' standings, with the pair almost making contact in the closing stages at the first chicane.

Antonelli took to the gravel on the exit, before recovering and blasting past Russell on the run to the Ascari chicane with four laps remaining.

"It was quite scary during the moment," he said.

"I thought I could still do the corner but once I went over a bit of gravel I went straight, and I was like maybe I've lost my chance, but then luckily we still had the pace and managed to bring it home."

title: Leclerc explains Monza crash and ‘too close’ Hamilton battle
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc has explained what caused his dramatic crash out of the Italian Grand Prix, with the Monegasque also giving his take on his “way too close” wheel-to-wheel battle with team mate Lewis Hamilton.

After starting from P3 and P4 on the grid – Leclerc ahead of Hamilton – the two Ferraris went side-by-side into the second corner as the race got underway.

Hamilton then had to take to the gravel and dropped backwards, leading the seven-time World Champion to suggest over the radio that he had been pushed off.

Leclerc’s subsequent charge did not last long as the 28-year-old ran off the track at Parabolica and into the barriers on Lap 2, putting him out of the race to the disappointment of the Tifosi watching on. Fortunately he was unharmed in the incident.

Speaking to the media later on, Leclerc firstly shared his thoughts on his fight with Hamilton and conceded that it is “never what you want” to see between team mates.

“With Lewis it was a way too close into Turn 1 and unfortunately in Turn 2 – I don't know if we had contact or whatsoever,” he explained.

“I was quite a lot on the inside curve and tried to make the corner, which I didn't do it tight enough, and then I obviously only saw in the mirrors what happened which is never what you want between two cars, between two cars of the same team.”

Reflecting on his exit from the race, Leclerc added: “Then for the crash itself, I went on throttle – on the first lap it felt kind of weird, I had to go back off and on throttle.

“On that second lap, I tried to do the same thing but, I don't know, it just felt a little bit weird, so we'll look into it.”

title: Duerksen sweeps Monza F2 weekend in Invicta Racing 1-2
excerpt:
Joshua Duerksen made it two race wins from two around Monza, winning the FIA Formula 2 Feature Race and leading home an Invicta Racing 1-2.

The Paraguayan driver started from P2 but took an early lead after team mate and polesitter Rafael Camara ran across Turn 2 on the opening lap, but the duelling Invictas then traded blows.

The lead changed hands multiple times before Duerksen pitted at the first opportunity to make the switch to soft tyres.

Camara opted to continue for a handful of laps but once the Brazilian made his pit stop, he emerged onto the track behind his team mate.

From there, Duerksen was in control, managing the gap behind and handling a mid-race Safety Car restart to retain his advantage out in front.

A late-race push from Camara put Duerksen under pressure, but the Scuderia Ferrari Driver Academy talent couldn’t find a way past before the chequered flag.

It marked Duerksen’s eighth win in F2, equalling the record jointly held by Felipe Drugovich, Nyck de Vries and Artem Markelov.

Camara took an important 18 points in the championship fight to move himself up to second in the standings and to within 11 points of leader Nikola Tsolov, who finished P7.

Noel Leon rounded out the podium for Campos Racing ahead of John Bennett and Ritomo Miyata in the top five.

title: Antonelli beats Russell to Italian GP win with stunning comeback
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli rose from the rear of the grid to claim victory in Sunday’s Italian Grand Prix, capping off a brilliant comeback drive by passing Mercedes team mate and title rival George Russell in the closing laps.

Antonelli started his home race down in 19th position after an engine penalty, with Russell on the front row of the grid, but the youngster rapidly climbed to the front of the field via a devastating blend of raw pace and smart overtaking.

A mid-race Virtual Safety Car played its part in the outcome, when Antonelli opted to pit under caution for a fresh set of medium tyres, and Russell stayed out on used hards, which gradually faded and made his life more difficult.

Aside from a brief trip through the gravel as he attacked Russell late on, Antonelli could not be faulted across 53 laps at the Autodromo Nazionale Monza – making another huge statement in his quest for the 2026 world title.

Russell had to settle for second place, crossing the line some four seconds behind Antonelli, while Red Bull’s Max Verstappen completed the podium finishers in a determined display that also featured several bold passes.

Lando Norris beat McLaren team mate Oscar Piastri to fourth via their own close fight, with Lewis Hamilton the lead Ferrari in sixth after team mate Charles Leclerc crashed heavily at the final corner on the second lap of the race.

After his breakthrough pole position, and a promising start, Pierre Gasly struggled to keep up with the front-runners and fell to seventh, as Arvid Lindblad, Franco Colapinto (who did well to recover from an off-track moment) and Yuki Tsunoda completed the points.

Gabriel Bortoleto and Nico Hulkenberg were next up in their Audi machines, the latter involved in a Turn 4 scrap with Liam Lawson that was looked at by the stewards, while Carlos Sainz took 13th for Williams.

The aforementioned Lawson ended his second substitute weekend for Red Bull in P14, ahead of Haas pair Ollie Bearman and Esteban Ocon, Albon in the other Williams and the Cadillacs of Sergio Perez and Valtteri Bottas.

Both Aston Martin drivers joined Leclerc on the sidelines later in the race – Fernando Alonso returning to the pits with suspected car damage and Lance Stroll pulling off the track due to a hydraulics issue.

AS IT HAPPENED

Gasly and Alpine delivered the shock of the season so far during Saturday’s Qualifying session at Monza, making the most of their recent chassis upgrades – and Mercedes power unit – to claim a sensational pole position.

Russell, beaten by Gasly in a game of online chess beforehand, took second position, with Piastri initially third before the stewards docked him three places on the grid for impeding Lawson in the Q2 phase.

That promoted Leclerc and Hamilton for an all-Ferrari second row, and Verstappen to fifth, while championship leader Antonelli dropped from seventh to the back of the grid due to his power unit-related penalty.

Albon and Lawson also served engine penalties, with Lawson later being required to start from the pit lane after changes to his Red Bull’s rear wing assembly under parc ferme conditions – Alonso joining him there due to his own post-Qualifying power unit changes.

As the 53-lap encounter approached, via a special demonstration run from Sebastian Vettel in Michael Schumacher’s 2002 Ferrari, intrigue grew as to whether or not Gasly would have the raw pace to convert his unexpected pole into victory.

There was also widespread expectation of early drama, given the different battery deployment patterns seen across teams and cars through Free Practice and Qualifying, and how that could lead to back-and-forth overtakes up and down the field.

Just before 1500 local time, with cars in position on the grid, it was revealed that Gasly and Russell would be starting the race on the medium tyre, while Leclerc, Hamilton and Verstappen all went more aggressive with the soft compound.

Other drivers on mediums were Piastri, Colapinto, Norris, Lindblad, Hulkenberg, Albon and Lawson, with Bortoleto, Bearman, Sainz, Ocon, Bottas, Perez and Stroll going for softs, and Tsunoda, Antonelli and Alonso choosing hards.

As the five red lights went out, polesitter Gasly made a smooth getaway to hold the lead over Russell into the first chicane, where Ferrari pair Leclerc and Hamilton went wheel-to-wheel – the latter seemingly forced into the gravel and tumbling down the order.

“Charles pushed me off!” Hamilton shouted over the radio a few moments later, as the seven-time World Champion briefly fell out of the points-paying positions. Behind, Piastri and Verstappen came close to contact themselves, as the Dutchman snuck ahead for P4.

Heading onto the second lap, Russell tucked in behind Gasly and made a clean move stick into the first chicane, where Leclerc also got ahead of the Alpine, only for the Frenchman to come back fighting into the second chicane and regain a place.

Drama then struck for Leclerc, who held a couple of slides in the middle sector and fell behind Verstappen, before losing control of his Ferrari exiting the Curva Alboreto and slamming into the barriers. Race Control initial deployed the Safety Car, before throwing a red flag.

Thankfully, Leclerc got out of his heavily damaged Ferrari unaided and looked to be unharmed. He then hopped over the barriers and crouched down – head in hands – in the shade, bringing back memories of Mika Hakkinen’s race-ending despair at Monza in 1999.

As the remaining 21 cars returned to the pits, Russell headed the queue from Gasly, Verstappen and a fast-starting Colapinto. McLaren pair Piastri and Norris held fifth and sixth, with Lindblad, Hamilton, Bearman and Ocon rounding out the top 10.

Antonelli had already worked his way up to 12th, splitting Audi duo Bortoleto and Hulkenberg, followed by Tsunoda, Lawson, Sainz, Perez, Albon and Bottas, as the Aston Martins of Stroll and Alonso completed the train.

After a period of barrier repairs, the pack headed out of the pits for a standing start. Most drivers were now on hards: Russell, Gasly, Colapinto, Piastri, Norris, Lindblad, Bearman, Ocon, Hulkenberg, Lawson, Sainz, Albon and Stroll. Meanwhile, Verstappen, Hamilton, Bortoleto, Antonelli, Tsunoda and Bottas were on mediums, and Perez and Alonso were on softs.

With Tsunoda missing his grid slot and lining up out of position, the start procedure was abandoned, meaning one more lap before the race got going again. When it did, Russell nailed his getaway to slot in front of Gasly, as Colapinto initially got the jump on Verstappen – only for the latter to reclaim P3 with a bold move at the second chicane.

Colapinto then hit trouble when he dramatically ran off the track and through the gravel at Lesmo 1, promoting the squabbling Hamilton and Piastri to P4 and P5. A lap later, the other Alpine of Gasly also lost ground when Verstappen charged past him down the back straight.

Incredibly, Antonelli was already up to seventh position, with his sights now set on the McLarens of Norris and Piastri – the Italian managing to edge in front of the reigning World Champion in an entertaining battle over the next few laps.

Lindblad, Tsunoda and Bearman held the final top-10 places, from Lawson, Hulkenberg, Ocon and Bortoleto, with Colapinto all the way down in 16th, between the Williams cars of Sainz and Albon, following his off-track excursion.

At the start of Lap 10, Gasly lost another position to Hamilton on the run down to the first chicane, before being swallowed up by Piastri and Antonelli in quick succession – the Alpine not enjoying quite so much pace in race conditions.

A couple of laps later, Verstappen jumped Russell for the lead at that popular first chicane overtaking spot, with Piastri also managing to make a move on Hamilton and get himself back into the podium places. Antonelli then followed Piastri through for P4 at the second chicane, as his phenomenal rise continued.

Despite his best efforts, Verstappen could not shake off Russell’s Mercedes as the race developed – the Briton fighting back to reclaim P1 into the second chicane on Lap 15, before Antonelli repeated the move on the four-time champion next time around.

“The car is completely broken on the rear axle,” reported Verstappen at this point, as he watched Antonelli close in on team mate Russell. When the trio headed onto Lap 18, Antonelli completed his back-of-the-grid charge by taking the lead from Russell into Turn 1.

Behind, Piastri and Hamilton continued their battle for fourth, ahead of Gasly, Norris, Lindblad, Tsunoda and Bearman. Bortoleto and Hulkenberg remained just outside the points – the latter involved in an incident with Lawson at Turn 4 that was noted and then dismissed by the stewards.

As predicted pre-race, the differing battery deployments led to a thrilling back-and-forth battle between Antonelli and Russell – the former falling behind at the first chicane and fighting back at the second chicane on multiple occasions.

TV cameras cut to Mercedes boss Toto Wolff in the middle of their squabble, with heart rates in the Mercedes garage no doubt raised when the team mates came perilously close to making contact through the Curva Grande on Lap 22.

“Kimi, we’re going to try and stop yo-yoing; we just need to build that gap to Verstappen,” was the message to Antonelli at this point. “Yeah right, and in the meantime, he passed me,” came the youngster’s response. “Do you want me just to sit behind, or what?”.

The tension stepped up a gear at the start of Lap 26 when Antonelli went too deep at the first chicane and ran over the inside strip of gravel – Verstappen continuing to watch on from third position, and ready to pounce on any opportunity.

Elsewhere, Alonso became the second retirement of the day due to suspected car damage. That became both Aston Martins when Stroll stopped with a hydraulic issue shortly afterwards. Hulkenberg, Ocon and Sainz pitted immediately, with Antonelli (taking on more mediums) and Verstappen (hards) doing the same a lap later.

Russell stayed out and pressed on in the lead, ahead of Piastri, Hamilton, Norris and Gasly, with Antonelli and Verstappen rejoining in P6 and P7, from Lindblad, Tsunoda and Bortoleto. Would this favour Russell in clear air? Or could Antonelli and Verstappen carve their way through the cars ahead?

Antonelli and Verstappen made light work of Gasly’s Alpine and Norris’ McLaren, putting them up to fourth and fifth almost immediately. With some 20 laps remaining, the pair sat just over 10 seconds away from race leader Russell, who was doing his best to pump in consistently quick times – and had been noted for a potential yellow flag infringement.

A mistake from Hamilton into the first chicane on Lap 35 handed another position to Antonelli. “Kimi 25.0,” Russell was told over the radio, in reference to his team mate’s lap times. “Just let me drive. I’m driving as quick as I can,” he firmly responded.

Only a lap later, Antonelli cleared Piastri into the first chicane for P2 – nine seconds now standing between himself and Russell, and a potential home win. Moments later, the stewards’ note involving Russell was ominously stepped up to a full investigation.

Behind the Silver Arrows, Verstappen slotted back into the podium places with overtakes on Hamilton and Piastri. Norris remained sixth, over Gasly, Lindblad and Tsunoda, while Colapinto had recovered to 10th and the final point on offer as things stood.

“Are the lap times good enough at the moment?” Russell asked over the radio with 15 laps to go. “Kimi’s forecast to catch [you] right at the end of the race,” came the response. But would Russell’s efforts all be undone by a penalty? The stewards’ subsequent ‘no further action’ message confirmed a straight fight to the chequered flag.

While Antonelli did all he could to catch Russell, more battling ensued between Verstappen and Piastri, and Norris and Hamilton, behind them – the positions changing several times and the action looking set to run and run over the closing tours.

“The tyre is opening up,” said Russell as he headed into the final 10 laps, with the concern in his voice growing. “Let’s take no risks. Just bring it home,” was the follow-up message from the Mercedes pit wall, as they braced for another intra-team scrap.

With five laps to go, Antonelli had Russell in his sights, and a move for the win looked inevitable. He got close heading into the first chicane on Lap 49, only to run wide at the exit, put all four wheels in the gravel and drop back.

Antonelli was not going to let the chance of a home win slip, however, and he soon recovered to challenge Russell once more – this time making a pass stick between Lesmo 2 and the Ascari chicane midway through Lap 50, and then storming into the distance.

While Antonelli duly confirmed victory over Russell, and Verstappen followed them home for a well-deserved podium, Norris grabbed fourth from team mate Piastri in a tight wheel-to-wheel moment through the Curva Grande – the Briton not impressed by such fine margins.

Hamilton salvaged sixth on a difficult day for Ferrari, from original P1 starter Gasly, Lindblad, Colapinto and Tsunoda, though the latter will be making a trip to the stewards post-race for a potential start procedure infringement.

Bortoleto and Hulkenberg followed for Audi, in front of Sainz, Lawson, the Haas cars of Bearman and Ocon, and Albon, while Perez and Bottas were the final drivers to reach the flag after Alonso, Stroll and Leclerc’s respective retirements.

Key quote

“Unbelievable! I’m so happy,” said Antonelli. “I could never have imagined to be here today, but we managed to pull it off. It’s a dream coming true. What an incredible day. I couldn’t do it without my team, family and everyone who supports me. Still a few races to go, so we’re going to keep our head down, but now we’re going to enjoy today.”

title: Why Monza has been second time unlucky for Lawson and Tsunoda
excerpt:
Liam Lawson and Yuki Tsunoda both impressed when they made substitute appearances at Zandvoort, particularly given the last-minute nature of the decision for Isack Hadjar to step aside.

It was a hugely important weekend for Tsunoda in particular, putting him back on the paddock’s radar. Lawson, meanwhile, is by no means guaranteed a race seat for 2027, with Nikola Tsolov waiting in the wings, and showing what he could do in a Red Bull strengthened his hand.

It was natural to assume that, given a second chance in Italy and a little more preparation, they would take another step forward. However, Monza has proved difficult for both so far and delivered something of a reality check.

Although it was not initially known to the wider world, Lawson came into the weekend knowing he'd have one hand tied behind his back after Red Bull decided to change power unit elements that would send him to the back of the grid.

That naturally meant a strong focus on race preparation in practice, but he still had the opportunity to earn a good position in Qualifying. Crucially, he was also tasked with giving team mate Max Verstappen a tow, a job Isack Hadjar performed so well at Spa.

In the end, Lawson did not complete his mission, managing only P13 in Q2 and failing to progress to Q3. It was a scrappy session for the New Zealander, made worse when Oscar Piastri impeded him at the start of his final run.

“It just wasn't ideal,” Lawson said. “We obviously left it to the end there to try and put a lap together. Tyres were pretty hot after just one cool, and then yeah, obviously not ideal getting blocked at Turn 1.

“I just spent the whole quali in clean air until that last lap, that was the first time I'd sat behind a car. So trying to do it for the first time was not ideal. But I think obviously having Oscar in Turn 1 probably hurt more than anything.”

He made his feelings clear on team radio about how things had unfolded.

“I mean, we just had a plan, and in some ways, we didn't really follow it exactly,” he said. “So for me, I just felt at times I didn't really know what I was doing. But obviously, for us this weekend quali wasn't really important for us."

Piastri hit with three-place grid penalty at Monza

Tsunoda meanwhile, is due to start from P15. The Racing Bulls driver qualified P17 after being knocked out in Q1, before penalties for other drivers moved him up the grid.

It was always going to be a tough weekend for Tsunoda, who had much to learn about energy management that had not been relevant at Zandvoort. On Friday, he acknowledged a lack of confidence and even admitted that at times he had forgotten to activate straight-line mode – something drivers do four times a lap at Monza.

He appeared to be making solid progress, but something clearly went wrong in Q1, with a 1.028-second gap to team mate Arvid Lindblad underlining the scale of the problem. After the session, Tsunoda was at a loss to explain it.

“There were some challenges through FP1 to FP3, something I can't control,” The Japanese racer said. “Qualifying it was probably bigger, but I appreciate the amount of work the team put in to solve that, and I understand it was very, very tight between FP3 and Qualifying. Hard to hear the answer, but I think something new happened in Qualifying.”

He added: “If you look first sector, I was like seven-tenths off, and there's only two corners.”

Tsunoda was adamant that by Qualifying he had a better understanding of the car.

“There were three sessions, and I explained a lot of things,” he said. “I don't think I've done anything massively wrong enough to lose lap time a lot, basically in the straight line, so I don't know. I have to hear the answer.

“But I appreciate the work of the team. I know the team is putting 100% effort and appreciate it. And also obviously that was pretty up and down sessions for me as well. There's obviously a lot of things on my side as well. But Qualifying I'm really curious, because the delta was pretty big.

“I'm pretty sure I didn't do any special things in Qualifying. I shouldn't be that slow, in my opinion. There are a lot of factors in Qualifying come in, because you have to get the slipstream and make the tow, and 95% or whatever on the throttle. But I think I've done a lot of things in practice, and it happen like this. So I want to hear answers.”

title: Stella on whether McLaren can still target Monza podium
excerpt:
Given that the team won the previous two races at the Hungaroring and Zandvoort, McLaren can hardly be satisfied with the outcome of a Monza Q3 session that left Oscar Piastri sixth on the grid and Lando Norris eighth.

The result was not representative of the car’s potential – Piastri initially qualified third before receiving a three-place grid penalty for impeding Liam Lawson in Q2 – and, despite the shortcomings of the MCL40 package, there remains potential to move forward in Sunday’s race.

That is the view of Team Principal Andrea Stella, who is taking a glass-half-full approach.

“Cars are very close to one another, so it's difficult for me to make a prediction for tomorrow,” he said on Saturday evening. “I think, in general, we should be able to compete for podiums, but we will have to be smart from a driving point of view, from an energy usage point of view, and from a strategic point of view.

“So there's certainly many variables, not necessarily all the ones that were relevant in Qualifying, but some of them yes, like actually being in a slipstream. We saw that in practice, for instance.”

So, what went wrong in Qualifying? As Stella explained, it was a question of suboptimal execution. That included Piastri’s costly impeding incident, which occurred as he left the pit lane towards the end of Q2, while Norris also highlighted issues with the brakes.

The frustration for McLaren was that both cars showed strong pace, with Piastri and Norris finishing second and third respectively in Q2.

“At times we executed well from a performance point of view,” said Stella. “Like in Q2, we had the two cars P1, P2, then they ended up P2, P3 at the end of Q2 because the cars were positioned in the right place in terms of slipstream, and both Oscar and Lando drove the cars very well despite the small gaps to the cars ahead.

“But yet in Q2 we managed to do an impeding. From an execution point of view, which is the wider aspect of going racing – which is not only pure car speed, there are several factors – and in Q2 we had this factor related to the impeding. Yet, performance seems to be competitive.

“We go in Q3. I think both cars in the first attempt were positioned well from a slipstream point of view. Probably Lando had too big a gap to the car ahead, I don't remember very well, but he loses some time in some corners. So in terms of execution, again, we leave some performance behind, while I think Oscar did a very good lap.”

Piastri hit with three-place grid penalty at Monza

Piastri’s first effort was good enough for third at that stage of the session. However, it was on the final run – when the McLarens were first out of the pit lane to avoid ending up at the back of the queue and potentially missing their laps – that things went awry.

“We had some issues managing the battery, and here in Monza, every 1% in the battery charge costs you a significant amount of milliseconds, and then we had the issue with Oscar locking corner one.

“So I think overall there's multiple areas in which we have not executed at the level that we should have, because in Monza, which is so peculiar, position of the car on track is as important as the underlying car performance, and also the management of the power unit and the brakes is once again as important as these other factors. So there was more that we could have achieved.”

Stella stressed that the car’s strong form at times at a circuit where straight-line performance is crucial gave the team encouragement.

“Actually, considering the process of setting up the car, optimization, chassis, driving, power unit, I think during Qualifying we saw that we had achieved a relatively competitive position,” he noted. “And like I referred to before, I think if we had done a better job of execution, had control of some parameters that don't only depend on the pure performance of the car, we could have definitely qualified, I would say, within the first couple of rows on the grid.

“So it's almost a half-pass from a performance point of view in terms of Monza being an exam that we wanted to use to test the performance of the MCL40.”

How that performance translates into race pace remains to be seen, but Stella is upbeat.

“Some of the factors that held us back today, I think, are not relevant tomorrow,” he said. “Like the slipstream, or the positioning on the car on track, or to some extent the brakes.

“It will be I think a very interesting race. Actually I am not sure that it's easy to think how it will unfold because it's a race in which if you start to play with the boost and overtake cars, you may get overtaken and you may start to lose overall time in the race.

“But at the same time, if you're faster, you may want to pass. Once again, I think being close to the car ahead will make you fast, and if you pass, you may be slower than you were after the car. It will be very interesting.”

title: Lando Norris issues 'fair' u-turn after Oscar Piastri radio frustration
excerpt:
Lando Norris has denied that Oscar Piastri's driving was out of line towards the end of the Italian Grand Prix.

The duo were involved in a late-race scrap for fourth place as McLaren looked to bring home a solid points haul after back-to-back victories at the last two rounds.

However, the race almost ended in disaster as, in the closing laps of the race, Norris attacked Piastri into Turn 4.

The reigning champion was forced to skate over the grass before settling back in behind his team-mate, expressing over team radio that he was pushed wide.

But Norris changed his tone after climbing out of the car, telling media including RacingNews365: “No, it was okay.

“I just need to review things, but it's just the perception of when you're in the car, when someone's opening the gap a bit and then goes straight.

“You get that perception when you're going at 200 miles per hour. So that's all.

“I think what he did was fair.”

Norris ended the race ahead of Piastri after moving in front of the Australian on the final lap with a move on the approach to the Ascari chicane.

Despite his team radio anger at the time, Norris insists he enjoyed the battle.

“It's just when you're in the moment, and you're half on the grass, you don't realise how quickly things can end pretty badly,” he said.

“Just in the heat of the moment, but no from that side, it was fine and it was a good battle. A good result from a tough race.”

title: Max Verstappen reveals Red Bull difficulty in Mercedes defeat: 'Wasn't our friend'
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has revealed that Red Bull struggled with top speed during the Italian Grand Prix, conceding that it "was not our friend" in defeat to Mercedes.

Verstappen started in fifth but quickly worked his way to the front, overtaking Lewis Hamilton, Charles Leclerc and Pierre Gasly.

The four-time world champion briefly led early in the race after passing George Russell, only for the Mercedes driver to quickly get back past.

Kimi Antonelli, starting from 19th, made rapid progress to the front and overtook Verstappen easily, with the two Silver Arrows drivers going on to break away.

Verstappen pitted during a mid-race virtual safety car for fresh hard tyres and did well to work his way back through from seventh to third, where he finished.

It was a positive result for the 28-year-old, who had to overtake several drivers around the outside due to Red Bull's straight-line struggles.

"There were some good battles out there," said Verstappen.

"I had to send it many times around the outside because we were just struggling a lot with deployment from turns two to four compared to our competitors.

"In general top speed wasn't our friend today so just tried to hang in there but they were just a bit too fast.

"That's why I was trying to be in that overtake mode but at one point I lost that and tried to just do my own race. Happy with P3 and to be on the podium here."

title: George Russell voices Mercedes surprise over decisive Kimi Antonelli pit stop call
excerpt:
George Russell has admitted surprise over Mercedes' decision to pit Kimi Antonelli during the virtual safety car period at Monza.

Russell held the lead of the race early on as he sought to close the gap in the standings to team-mate Kimi Antonelli, who started from 19th place.

title: Kimi Antonelli names 'scary' moment he thought 'he lost his chance' to win historic Italian GP
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli has named the "scary" moment he thought he lost his chance to win the Italian Grand Prix - and take a giant step towards winning the world championship title.

Antonelli passed George Russell on Lap 50 of 53 to win by 3.8s, becoming the first driver to win from 19th on the grid since Bill Vukovich at the 1954 Indianapolis 500.

He is the first Italian to win his home grand prix since Ludovico Scarfiotti for Ferrari in 1966, and now leads the drivers' standings by 66 points from Russell, whom Antonelli defeated in combat.

On Lap 49, Antonelli was forced wide at Turn 2 into the gravel but recovered to sweep past Russell and take the seventh win of his career, and the 50th overall for an Italian driver.

Reflecting, the 20-year-old, recalled the scare of going off as the track began to break up.

"Unbelievable, unbelievable. I'm so happy, and I could have never imagined to to be here today," he said.

"But we managed to pull it off, and I'm really, really happy.

"It was quite scary there in the moment because the tarmac was breaking up, but I still thought I could do the corner. But once I went over a bit of gravel as well, I went straight, and I was like, maybe I've lost my chance.

"But then, luckily, we still had the pace and managed to bring it home.

"After the second restart, I was up there, and I knew I could have had a shot for the win. So yeah, definitely I believed in it, especially when I was behind George.

"But it was really difficult to break away, we pitted, and he stayed out, and he struggled a bit with his tyres at the end, while with fresher tyres, I was able to increase the pace and managed to win."

title: Kimi Antonelli victory brilliance triggers Monza eruption in red-flagged Italian GP
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli completed a remarkable 19th to first recovery to win the Italian Grand Prix, in what was a red-flagged race in Monza.

A red flag was required on the third lap after a huge accident for Charles Leclerc at Parabolica, resulting in barrier repairs being required.

Yo-yo racing again took centre stage, with George Russell being forced to settle for second despite leading large portions of the race.

Max Verstappen completed the podium ahead of both McLarens, while Lewis Hamilton finished in a disappointing sixth. Polesitter Pierre Gasly ended up in seventh.

Horror Ferrari start

It was near-impossible to decide where to look on the Monza grid, with Pierre Gasly on pole but championship leader Kimi Antonelli down in 19th.

There was a real mix of starting tyre compounds. Gasly and George Russell on the front row opted for new mediums, while Charles Leclerc, Lewis Hamilton and Max Verstappen all went for new softs.

As the lights went out, it was the front-row duo who got away best and remained first and second, while Hamilton tried to overtake Leclerc at the first corner.

It went badly for the Briton, who was then on the outside at Turn 2, where Leclerc forced him fairly onto the gravel. Hamilton tumbled to 10th as a result and immediately complained on the radio.

The start quickly worsened for Ferrari, as a lap later Verstappen overtook Leclerc, before the Monegasque suffered a scary crash at the final corner.

He found himself under pressure from Oscar Piastri and was forced to take a different line into Parabolica at the end of the second lap. Leclerc went wide and touched the drain on the outside of the white line, catching him off guard and sending him into the wall at high speed.

It initially triggered a safety car, but this was quickly escalated to a full red flag. A lengthy 30-minute stoppage took place to recover Leclerc's car and repair the barrier.

Elsewhere, before the red flag, Russell overtook Gasly at the first corner on lap two for the lead. It meant that at the race restart, Russell was on pole, ahead of Gasly, Verstappen, Franco Colapinto and Piastri. Hamilton was eighth, with Antonelli incredibly up to 12th.

Race restart and Antonelli brilliance

Crucially, the red flag allowed the entire field to change tyres, in what was predicted by Pirelli to be only a one-stop race. It meant that nobody needed to pit again unless they desired to.

Russell, Gasly, Colapinto and both McLarens in fifth and sixth opted for new hard tyres, while Verstappen, Hamilton and Antonelli chose new mediums. Unfortunately, the restart was aborted due to Yuki Tsunoda being out of position.

Thankfully, the lights did go out to restart the race at the beginning of lap six, with Russell and Gasly safely remaining in first and second.

It was all change behind, as Verstappen overtook Colapinto for third at Turn 4, before the Argentinian went off at Turn 6 and fell to 16th. Hamilton also made a strong restart, rising from eighth to fourth.

Antonelli's restart was also unbelievable, as the title leader found himself in sixth by the end of lap seven. Meanwhile, Gasly fell to third behind Verstappen.

Third became fourth for Gasly at the start of lap 10, as Hamilton roared past the Frenchman at the entry of the opening corner. The Tifosi let off an almighty cheer. It was a disastrous lap for Gasly, as Piastri and Antonelli also got past.

Yo-yo racing chaos unfolded over the next eight laps. On lap 12, Verstappen passed Russell for the lead, while Piastri and Antonelli both overtook Hamilton. A lap later, Antonelli got past the McLaren for third.

Lap 15, and Russell regained the lead from Verstappen, with the Dutchman slipping to third a lap later behind Antonelli. The two Mercedes quickly started battling and swapping positions, but come lap 29, it was Russell ahead of the Italian.

A virtual safety car was triggered on that lap after Lance Stroll came to a halt at the first corner, joining his team-mate out of the race. Crucially, Antonelli and Verstappen both pitted, the former for new mediums and the latter for new hards.

The duo rejoined in sixth and seventh and made rapid progress. By lap 37, Antonelli was back into second and just nine seconds behind Russell. In a significant moment on lap 38, Russell was placed under investigation for a yellow-flag infringement, but no further action was taken.

As the race entered its final 10 laps, Russell held a 5.5s lead over Antonelli, with Verstappen, Piastri, Norris and Hamilton completing the top six.

Concerningly for Russell, his tyres started to open up, allowing his team-mate to get onto his rear with a handful of laps remaining. Ultimately, with his degrading tyres, Russell had no answer to Antonelli on fresher rubber.

However, Antonelli's first attempt at overtaking went badly wrong on lap 49, with him going off into the gravel but managing to safely rejoin. Antonelli's next attempt came on lap 50, this time to great success.

Russell had to settle for second, with Antonelli cruising into the distance to pick up an emotional win on home soil. Verstappen, Norris and Piastri completed the top five.

title: Charles Leclerc reveals 'vision' problems after massive Monza crash
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc says he suffered from initial vision problems in the immediate aftermath of his huge Italian Grand Prix accident - and that he will undergo further precautionary checks ahead of the Spanish GP next week.

On Lap 3 at Monza, Leclerc was battling with the McLaren of Oscar Piastri around the Parabolica when he lost control and speared into the barriers.

The Monegasque was able to climb unaided from the car and was quickly attended to trackside by the FIA doctors, and undertook a mandatory trip to the medical centre after triggering the G-sensors onboard the car.

He was given a clean bill of health and quickly released to carry out his media duties, where he revealed initial vision problems after the impact.

"It was just my vision a little bit at first; the right eye was not showing me great vision," Leclerc told media, including RacingNews365.

"But now it's all good. That's the thing I was most worried of getting out of the car; then, after that, everything was a bit of pain here and there, which is normal after a crash like this. So nothing more.

"I think from Lap 1 to Lap 2, I had a bit of a difference in power delivery. We'll look into it, but I don't want to comment too much before checking the data and confirm it.”

It marked a hugely disappointing outcome for Ferrari at its home event, having entered the round hoping to challenge at the front of the field.

While frustrated, Leclerc voiced hope that he will have better fortunes next time out in Madrid, should he be cleared to race.

"This is obviously the biggest race of the year for the team, and a lot of fans here cheering for you. Yeah, it's it's very frustrating, but it's the way it's the way it is now.

"I cannot change the results. I'll have to look forward and hopefully bounce back in Madrid.

"I think I'll have quite a few additional checks that we still have to do on my side, probably tonight and tomorrow to make sure that I'll be fully fine for Madrid.

"It should be the case, but yeah, better be safe than sorry."

title: Pierre Gasly, George Russell facing disadvantage to F1 rivals at Italian GP
excerpt:
Pierre Gasly and George Russell both face a potential disadvantage at the Italian Grand Prix - in that they have no new soft tyres left.

The front-row pair head into the race with only new medium and new hard tyres, locking them into one of Pirelli's pre-race predictions of a medium-hard strategy, stopping between Laps 24-30 of 53 for the sole stop.

However, all of those around the front-row, including both Ferraris from the second row, have a new set of softs, a new medium, and a new hard to choose from, opening up more strategy variations.

One such is to start on the softs until Laps 19-25 before switching to mediums, or alternatively, running the mediums from the start until Laps 30-36, before a short blast to the flag.
